meanings: to use; to make use of; to employ

example.english: I use chopsticks to eat.
example.fact: 筷子 (chopsticks) have been used in China for thousands of years.

components.note: 辶 (to walk) — 道 relates to a path or road one walks along.
首 (shǒu) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading no longer resembles dào, a reminder that sound components can drift after thousands of years of pronunciation change.

example.english: Laozi wrote the Dao De Jing.
example.fact: Laozi is traditionally regarded as the founder of Daoism, and the Dao De Jing is one of the most influential texts in Chinese philosophy.

etymologyHint: To take small steps 亍 with one's feet 彳

components.note: 彳 depicts a step with the left foot; together with 亍 (a step with the right foot), 行 shows a person walking or moving.
亍 depicts a step with the right foot, complementing 彳 to form the idea of walking or travel.

example.english: Marco Polo liked to travel.
example.fact: Marco Polo was a Venetian merchant whose 13th-century travels through China became famous after being recorded in a widely read travelogue.

meanings: classifier for houses, small buildings, institutions etc
etymologyHint: An axe 斤 swung at a door 户

components.note: 户 (door) — 所 evokes a location or place, such as where a door stands.
斤 (axe) — combined with 户 (door), the image of an axe at a door gave rise to the abstract sense of 'a place' or 'that which.'

example.hanzi: 北京大学是一所有名的大学。
example.pinyin: Běijīng Dàxué shì yì suǒ yǒumíng de dàxué.
example.english: Peking University is a well-known university.
example.fact: Peking University, founded in 1898, is one of the oldest and most prestigious universities in China.

components.note: 灬 (fire) — 然 originally described burning; the meaning later shifted to 'so, correct' as 然 became a grammatical particle.
肰 (rán) gives the sound — 然 is also pronounced rán, an exact match.

example.english: Of course, the Earth is round.
example.fact: The Earth is a sphere, though it bulges slightly at the equator.

meanings: used in 傢伙|家伙[jia1 huo5] and 傢俱|家俱[jia1 ju4]

components.note: 宀 (roof) — 家 is about a home, the space under a roof.
豕 (shǐ, 'pig') supplies the ancient sound for 家; keeping a pig under one's roof was also a practical sign of a household in ancient China, though the modern readings jiā and shǐ no longer rhyme.

example.english: The panda's home is in China.
example.fact: Giant pandas are native to China, living mainly in mountain forests in Sichuan province.

components.note: 禾 (grain/rice plant) — 种 relates to seeds and planting crops.
中 (zhōng) gives the sound — 种 is pronounced zhǒng, matching aside from tone.

example.hanzi: 大米是一种重要的食物。
example.pinyin: Dàmǐ shì yì zhǒng zhòngyào de shíwù.
example.english: Rice is an important kind of food.
example.fact: Rice is a staple food for more than half of the world's population.

example.pinyin: Dúshū shì yí jiàn hǎo shì.
example.english: Reading is a good thing.
example.fact: In Mandarin, abstract matters or affairs are often counted with the measure word 件, as in 一件事 ('a matter').

meanings: short name for Chengdu 成都[Cheng2 du1]

example.english: Chengdu has many pandas.
example.fact: Chengdu, the capital of Sichuan province, is home to several well-known giant panda breeding and research centers.

example.hanzi: 故宫是一个有名的地方。
example.pinyin: Gùgōng shì yí gè yǒumíng de dìfāng.
example.english: The Forbidden City is a famous place.
example.fact: The Forbidden City in Beijing served as the imperial palace for the Ming and Qing dynasties for almost 500 years.

meanings: many; much; more; a lot of

components.note: 夕 (evening/night), doubled — two nights stacked together suggested the idea of accumulation, giving 多 its meaning of 'many, much.'

example.english: China has many people.
example.fact: China is one of the most populous countries in the world.

components.note: 纟 (silk/thread) — 经 originally referred to the vertical warp threads in weaving.
工 (gōng) gives a related sound cue for 经 (jīng), reflecting an older, closer pronunciation link between the two.

example.english: He passes by the park every day.
example.fact: 经 originally referred to the vertical warp threads in weaving (reflected in its 纟 'silk/thread' radical), and later broadened to mean 'to pass through' and 'classic texts.'

meanings: suffix, used to form interrogative 什麼|什么[shen2 me5], what?, indefinite 這麼|这么[zhe4 me5] thus, etc

example.english: What is this?
example.fact: 么 has no meaning of its own — it's a grammatical suffix that appears in question words like 什么 (shénme, 'what') and demonstratives like 这么 (zhème, 'like this').

example.english: I want to go to the Great Wall.
example.fact: The Great Wall of China stretches for thousands of kilometers across northern China.

etymologyHint: The course 去 followed by a stream 氵

components.note: 氵 (water/stream) — water naturally follows a fixed course, an image linked to the idea of 'law' or 'method.'
去 (to go/a course) — the path a stream follows suggested a regulated, consistent way of doing things, hence 'law, method.'

example.english: France is in Europe.
example.fact: France is a country in Western Europe, well known for landmarks like the Eiffel Tower.

etymologyHint: A building 冖 where children 子 study, with an additional graphic element ⺍ at the top

components.note: 冖 (a covering/roof) — represents the building or schoolhouse where learning happens.
子 (child) — 学 depicts children gathered to study.
⺍ is a small graphic element at the top of the character; its original pictorial meaning, if any, has been lost over time.

example.english: Confucius liked to study.
example.fact: Confucius was an ancient Chinese philosopher whose teachings have shaped Chinese culture and education for over 2,000 years.

etymologyHint: A wife 女 following her husband's words 口

components.note: 女 (woman) — depicts a wife in the traditional image behind this character.
口 (mouth/words) — the wife following her husband's spoken words gave 如 its meaning of 'as, like, if.'

example.hanzi: 如果你饿了,你可以吃饭。
example.pinyin: Rúguǒ nǐ è le, nǐ kěyǐ chī fàn.
example.english: If you're hungry, you can eat.
example.fact: 如 combines 女 (woman) and 口 (mouth) — the character's core meaning of 'as, like, if' comes from the old image of following someone's spoken words.

components.note: 阝 (a variant of 邑, meaning city/settlement) — 都 relates to a capital or metropolis.
者 (zhě) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading no longer closely matches dōu, reflecting centuries of sound change.

example.english: We are all students.
example.fact: 都 (dōu) is an adverb meaning 'all' or 'both,' and in Mandarin it always comes before the verb, never after the noun it refers to.

etymologyHint: Sharing a common 凡 tongue 口

components.note: 凡 (common/ordinary) — suggests something shared or held in common.
口 (mouth) — sharing a common mouth/voice with others gave 同 its meaning of 'same, together.'

example.english: We are classmates.
example.fact: 同学 combines 同 ('same') and 学 ('to study') — literally 'one who studies together with you,' the Mandarin word for 'classmate.'

etymologyHint: To see 见 jade 王

components.note: 王 (a variant of 玉, meaning jade) — a valuable object one might glimpse or notice.
见 (to see) — catching sight of something links to the meanings 'to appear, present, now.'

example.english: It's three o'clock now.
example.fact: 现 combines 王 (a form of 玉, 'jade') and 见 ('to see') — the image of jade catching the light gave rise to the meaning 'to appear,' later extended to 'now, present.'

example.english: She wants to be a doctor.
example.fact: 当, when used before a profession, means 'to work as' or 'to serve as' — as in 当医生 (to be a doctor) or 当老师 (to be a teacher).

meanings: (negative prefix for verbs) have not; not

components.note: 氵 (water) — 没 originally meant to sink or drown in water, later extended to the negative 'not have.'
殳 (shū) is the historical sound component; it no longer rhymes with méi in modern Mandarin, another case of sound drift over time.

example.english: I don't have money.
example.fact: 没 is the special negation word used only with 有 ('to have') — Mandarin uses 不 to negate almost every other verb, but 没有 is the exception.

components.note: 力 (strength/force) — 动 relates to movement produced by exertion or force.

example.english: Exercise is good for the body.
example.fact: Regular exercise strengthens the heart and lungs and is one of the most reliable ways to improve long-term health.

components.note: 面 was originally a pictograph of a human face, with an outline around an eye — later broadening to mean 'face, surface, side.'

example.pinyin: Dìqiú de biǎomiàn yǒu hěn duō shuǐ.
example.english: The Earth's surface has a lot of water.
example.fact: About 70% of Earth's surface is covered by water.

components.note: 走 (to walk/run) — 起 relates to standing up and setting into motion.
己 (jǐ) gives a close sound cue — 起 is pronounced qǐ, sharing the same final sound.

example.english: The sun rises from the east.
example.fact: Because of Earth's rotation, the sun always appears to rise in the east and set in the west.

etymologyHint: Shielding one's eyes 目 with a hand 手 to look to the distance

components.note: 手 (hand) — depicts a hand raised above the eyes.
目 (eye) — shielding the eyes with a hand to look into the distance gave 看 its meaning 'to look, to see.'

example.hanzi: 很多中国人喜欢看《西游记》。
example.pinyin: Hěn duō Zhōngguórén xǐhuān kàn Xīyóu Jì.
example.english: Many Chinese people like to read Journey to the West.
example.fact: Journey to the West is one of the Four Great Classical Novels of Chinese literature.

meanings: to fix; to set; to make definite
to subscribe to (a newspaper etc); to book (tickets etc); to order (goods etc)
etymologyHint: A person 疋 settling under a roof 宀

components.note: 宀 (roof) — represents a home or fixed dwelling.
疋 (a foot/person) — a person settling down under a roof gave 定 its meaning 'to decide, to fix, to settle.'

example.english: He decided to study Chinese.
example.fact: 定 originally depicted a person settling down under a roof, which is how it came to mean 'to decide' or 'to fix in place.'

etymologyHint: The heavens 一 above a man 大

components.note: 大 (a person, arms outstretched) — represents a human being.
一 (a line, here representing the sky) — drawn above a person, showing what is above them: the heavens, hence 'sky, day.'

example.english: The sky is blue.
example.fact: The sky looks blue because air molecules scatter blue light from the sun more strongly than other colors, a phenomenon called Rayleigh scattering.

meanings: (bound form) branch of (an organization); sub- (as in 分局[fen1 ju2])
etymologyHint: Pieces 八 being further subdivided with a knife 刀

components.note: 八 (to divide/split apart) — represents something already split into parts.
刀 (knife) — a knife cutting already-divided pieces further, giving 分 its meaning 'to divide, to separate.'

example.pinyin: Yí gè xiǎoshí yǒu liùshí fēnzhōng.
example.english: An hour has sixty minutes.
example.fact: An hour is defined as sixty minutes, a division of time used all over the world.

components.note: 辶 (to walk/move) — relates to motion or progress.
不 (not) — 'not yet moving on' gave 还 its meaning of 'still, yet.'

example.english: He still hasn't eaten yet.
example.fact: 还 (hái) is a polyphonic character — as hái it means 'still' or 'also,' but as huán it means 'to return something,' a completely different word with the same written form.

components.note: 辶 (to walk) — 进 relates to advancing or entering, both movement-related.
井 (jǐng) gives a close sound cue — 进 is pronounced jìn, sharing similar consonant and vowel sounds.

example.pinyin: Tā xué Zhōngwén, jìnbù hěn kuài.
example.english: He studies Chinese and is progressing quickly.
example.fact: 进 is one of the most common directional complements in Mandarin, appearing in words like 进来 (come in) and 进去 (go in) to show movement toward or away from a place.

etymologyHint: A woman 女 with a son 子

components.note: 女 (woman) — represents a mother.
子 (child/son) — a mother together with her child was seen as an image of goodness, giving 好 its meaning 'good.'

example.english: Tea is good for the body.
example.fact: Tea originated in China thousands of years ago and remains one of the most widely consumed beverages in the world today.

etymologyHint: Dividing 八 by a line 亅

components.note: 八 (to divide/split) — represents something being separated into smaller parts.
亅 (a hook/line) — cutting a small piece off, an image tied to the meaning 'small, tiny.'

example.english: Baby pandas are very small.
example.fact: Newborn giant pandas are extremely small, weighing only about 100 grams — roughly 1/900th of their mother's weight.

components.note: 阝 (a variant of 邑, meaning place/settlement) — 部 relates to a division, section, or department.
咅 supplies the sound for 部 (bù); it belongs to the same phonetic family as related characters like 倍 (bèi) and 培 (péi).

example.pinyin: Sānguó Yǎnyì shì yí bù xiǎoshuō.
example.english: Romance of the Three Kingdoms is a novel.
example.fact: Romance of the Three Kingdoms is one of the Four Great Classical Novels of Chinese literature, based on events from China's Three Kingdoms period.

example.pinyin: Wǒ yào mǎi qítā de shū.
example.english: I want to buy other books.
example.fact: 其 is a classical Chinese pronoun meaning 'his, her, its, their' — today it mostly survives inside words like 其他 ('other') and 其中 ('among them') rather than standing alone.

meanings: classifier indicating a small amount or small number greater than 1: some, a few, several

components.note: 二 (two) — 些 originally suggested a small plural amount, building on the idea of 'more than one.'
此 (cǐ) is the historical phonetic element; it no longer closely matches the modern reading xiē.

example.english: There are some books on the table.
example.fact: 些 acts as a plural marker after words like 一, 这, and 那 (as in 一些, 这些, 那些) — Mandarin nouns themselves don't change form to show plural the way English nouns do.

etymologyHint: A lamp 王 with a flame 丶

components.note: 丶 (a dot) — represents the burning flame atop a lamp.
王 here depicts the base and stand of an oil lamp, not its usual meaning 'king' — the one who tends the flame became linked to 'master, lord, main.'

example.pinyin: Tā shì zhège jiā de zhǔrén.
example.english: He is the head of this family.
example.fact: 主 originally depicted an oil lamp with a burning flame — a fitting image for 'master' or 'lord,' the person who tends and controls the flame of the household.

components.note: 木 (tree/wood) — 样 originally referred to a kind of tree, later broadening to mean 'kind, appearance, way.'
羊 (yáng) gives the sound — 样 is pronounced yàng, matching aside from tone.

example.pinyin: Zhè liǎng gè píngguǒ bù yíyàng.
example.english: These two apples are not the same.
example.fact: 一样 (yíyàng, 'the same') is one of the most common ways to compare two things in Mandarin, usually in the pattern 跟...一样 or 不一样.

components.note: 王 (a variant form of 玉, meaning jade) — 理 originally referred to the natural grain or pattern in jade, later extending to 'reason, logic, to manage.'
里 (lǐ) gives the sound — 理 is also pronounced lǐ, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Dìlǐ shì yì mén yǒuqù de kè.
example.english: Geography is an interesting subject.
example.fact: Geography is the study of Earth's physical features, climate, and the distribution of living things across the planet.

components.note: 心 was originally a pictograph of the physical shape of a human heart, and came to represent the mind, feelings, and intention as well.

example.english: The heart is on the left side of the body.
example.fact: The human heart sits slightly left of center in the chest and beats around 100,000 times every day.

etymologyHint: A woman 女 beside you 也

components.note: 女 (woman) — marks this pronoun as specifically feminine.
也 was already used as a gender-neutral third-person pronoun; adding 女 to it created a new character specifically for 'she.'

example.english: She is my teacher.
example.fact: 她 ('she') is a modern character, created in the early 20th century by Chinese writers who added 女 ('woman') to the existing pronoun 也 specifically to translate the Western grammatical distinction between 'he' and 'she.'

etymologyHint: A tree 木 with its roots highlighted

components.note: 木 (tree) — provides the base image of a tree.
一 (a line) marks the base of the trunk, highlighting the roots — giving 本 its meaning 'root, origin, source.'

example.pinyin: Lúnyǔ shì yì běn zhòngyào de shū.
example.english: The Analects is an important book.
example.fact: The Analects records the teachings of Confucius and has shaped Chinese thought and education for more than two thousand years.

example.english: The teacher stands in front of the classroom.
example.fact: In Mandarin, spatial words for 'front' and 'back' often double as time words — 以前 (yǐqián) means 'before' in time, while 前面 (qiánmiàn) means 'in front' in space, both built on 前.

meanings: (of ships, vehicles, troops etc) to start
etymologyHint: Simplified form of 開; hands 廾 lifting the latch 一 of a door

components.note: 廾 (two hands) — depicts hands at work.
一 represents the latch or bar of a door; hands lifting it away gave 开 its meaning 'to open, to start.'

example.english: He drives to work every day.
example.fact: 开 is the simplified form of 開, which originally showed two hands lifting the bar of a gate — a vivid image behind its meaning 'to open' or 'to start.'

components.note: 旦 (dàn) gives the sound — 但 is also pronounced dàn, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Wǒ hěn lèi, dànshì wǒ hěn kāixīn.
example.english: I'm very tired, but I'm very happy.
example.fact: 但是 (dànshì) is the most common way to say 'but' in Mandarin; 但 alone can also express the same meaning in slightly more formal or literary contexts.

example.hanzi: 因为下雨,所以我们不去公园。
example.pinyin: Yīnwèi xià yǔ, suǒyǐ wǒmen bù qù gōngyuán.
example.english: Because it's raining, we're not going to the park.
example.fact: 因为...所以... (yīnwèi...suǒyǐ..., 'because...so...') is a distinctive Mandarin pattern — unlike English, both connecting words are commonly used together in the same sentence.

etymologyHint: Simple words 八 coming from the mouth 口

components.note: 口 (mouth) — the source of speech.
八 here suggests something small or simple leaving the mouth, giving 只 its meaning 'only, merely.'

example.pinyin: Tā zhǐ hē shuǐ, bù hē kāfēi.
example.english: He only drinks water, not coffee.
example.fact: 只 is polyphonic: as zhǐ it means 'only,' but as zhī it's the measure word for animals (一只猫, 'one cat') — the same character doing two unrelated jobs depending on its tone.

components.note: 人 (person), doubled — one person shown following another depicts the idea of accompanying or coming from somewhere.

example.english: He comes from Beijing.
example.fact: 从...到... (cóng...dào..., 'from...to...') is the standard Mandarin pattern for describing a range, whether in space (from one city to another) or in time (from one day to another).

components.note: 心 (heart/mind) — 想 relates to thinking, missing someone, or wanting something in one's heart.
相 (xiāng) gives the sound — 想 is pronounced xiǎng, matching aside from tone.

example.english: I want to travel to China.
example.fact: 想 combines 心 ('heart/mind') and 相 ('appearance') — reflecting the old idea that thinking means picturing something in the mind's eye.

example.english: This is a fact.
example.fact: 事实 (shìshí, 'fact') combines 事 ('matter') and 实 ('real, solid') — literally 'a real/solid matter.'
